title.source: How can letters challenge limits on learning?

essentialQuestion.source: What can Kartini's letters tell us about hopes for girls' schooling in colonial Java, and what can an official record add?

learningGoal.source: Use a letter and an official record to explain Kartini's hope for girls' schooling, and keep a hope, a decision and an outcome apart.

warmUp.question.source: Which tells you more about what a person hoped for?

evidence.question.source: Which source records a hope, which records a decision, and which only shows a face?

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.caption.source: Source 1: Kartini's letter to a friend, begun on 11 October 1901 and finished on 24 October 1901

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.0.source: Kartini wrote it in Dutch. We read it as letter 26 in Letters of a Javanese Princess, an English translation by Agnes Louise Symmers, first published in London in 1921.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.1.source: In it, Kartini says she and her sisters hope to open a school that teaches more than books: handwork, home skills, wood-carving and painting.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.2.source: In the same letter, she describes a different plan: the colonial government's plan for girls' schools, including one for daughters of noble families, where she was asked to teach.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.3.source: Limit: an editor chose which letters to publish years after her death, and the English book has only about two-thirds of them. It is a selected translation, not her exact words.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.caption.source: Source 2: A government decision, 7 July 1903 (National Archives of Indonesia)

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.0.source: The colonial government agreed to give Kartini and her sister Roekmini 4,800 guilders to study in Batavia, now Jakarta.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.1.source: Kartini's own letter of 24 July 1903, and a note by the editor of her letters, both mention this decision.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.2.source: Limit: a decision shows what officials agreed to. It does not prove anyone used the money. The sisters did not use it.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.caption.source: Source 3: A portrait of Kartini, printed in a book in 1922

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.0.source: It comes from Habis Gelap Terbitlah Terang, a translation of her letters into Malay, published in 1922. The photographer is not known.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.1.source: In 2021, a Wikimedia Commons user called FenyMufyd cropped it and cleaned it up digitally.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.2.source: Limit: it shows her face. It cannot show her thoughts, or when the photo was taken.

evidence.cards.1.title.source: A hope, a decision and what happened

evidence.cards.1.events.0.text.source: Kartini is born in Jepara, on the island of Java.

evidence.cards.1.events.1.text.source: In a letter, Kartini writes about her and her sisters' hope to open a school (Source 1).

evidence.cards.1.events.2.text.source: The colonial government agrees to pay for Kartini and Roekmini to study in Batavia (Source 2).

evidence.cards.1.events.3.text.source: Kartini and her sisters teach a few girls at home, her letters say.

evidence.cards.1.events.4.text.source: The sisters do not use the money. Kartini marries the regent of Rembang.

evidence.cards.1.events.6.text.source: A selection of her letters is published in Dutch, and later in English.

evidence.cards.1.events.7.text.source: A Malay translation of her letters is printed, with her portrait (Source 3).

read.sections.0.heading.source: A letter writer in colonial Java

read.sections.0.text.source: Raden Ajeng Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara, on the island of Java. At that time, the Netherlands ruled Java as a colony. Her father was a local leader, and she went to school until she was about 12. That was more schooling than most girls in Java had. Then, like other girls from noble families, she had to stay at home until she married. She kept reading, and she wrote many letters, mostly in Dutch, to friends. She wrote about why girls should be able to learn and choose their own path. A letter shows one person's hopes. It cannot speak for every girl in Java. Today her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Kartini was born in 1879 on the island of Java. The Netherlands ruled Java then. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until she was about 12. Then she had to stay at home. She wrote many letters to friends. She wrote that girls should be able to learn. A letter shows what one person hoped. It does not speak for every girl. Today her letters are kept in an archive.

read.sections.1.text.source: In October 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter to a friend. She wrote that she and her sisters hoped to open a school one day. It would teach more than books: handwork, cooking, wood-carving and painting too. In the same letter, she wrote about a different plan. The colonial government was planning schools for girls, and Kartini had been asked to teach in one. These were two plans, not one. We can read her letter in an English translation from 1921. Years after her death, an editor chose which letters to print, and the English book kept only some of them.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 1901, Kartini wrote a long letter. She and her sisters hoped to open a school. It would teach books, and also cooking and art. In the same letter, she wrote about another plan. The government planned schools for girls. It asked Kartini to teach. These were two different plans. We read the letter in an English translation from 1921. An editor chose which letters to print. So we do not have all her words.

read.sections.2.text.source: On 7 July 1903, the colonial government made a decision. It offered Kartini and her sister Roekmini a scholarship, money to study in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta. A record of this decision is kept in Indonesia's national archive. A decision shows what officials agreed to at one moment. It does not prove that anyone used the money. In fact, the sisters did not use it, and later that year Kartini married. The second picture is her portrait, printed in a book in 1922, long after her death. It shows her face, not her thoughts.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: On 7 July 1903, the government made a decision. It gave Kartini and her sister a scholarship. This was money to study in Batavia, now called Jakarta. An archive in Indonesia keeps the decision. A decision shows what leaders agreed. It does not show what happened next. The sisters did not use the money. The second picture is a portrait of Kartini. It was printed in 1922. It shows her face, not her thoughts.

write.example.source: Kartini hoped girls could learn more. In her 1901 letter, she wrote about a school she and her sisters hoped to open. It would teach books, cooking and art. In 1903, the government offered Kartini and Roekmini a scholarship to study in Batavia. But the decision does not prove she used it, and the sisters did not. One limit of the letter is that an editor chose it, and we read it in translation.

speak.partnerTask.source: With a partner, talk about how a letter and an official record answer different questions. Each of you names one question the letter answers and one the decision answers.

speak.independentTask.source: Make a note with two columns: “The letter tells us” and “The decision tells us”. Write two points in each column, then read them aloud.

watch.summary.source: This short film comes from a library in Leiden, in the Netherlands. The library keeps many of Kartini's letters. The film is about her letters. Kartini was born in 1879 in Jepara, on the island of Java. At that time, the Netherlands ruled Java. Her father was a local leader. She went to school until she was about 12. Then she had to stay at home until she married. She kept reading, and she wrote many letters to friends. Most were in Dutch. In them, she wrote about why girls should be able to learn. Today her letters are kept in archives in the Netherlands and Indonesia. This written version comes from the library's own page, not from the film.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Kartini's life touches on things that can be personal: girls kept at home, arranged marriage (her husband already had other wives), and her death a few days after giving birth. The lesson says only that she married in 1903; if the rest comes up, keep it brief and factual. Many learners have had their own schooling interrupted: keep the lesson on Kartini's sources, and never ask learners whether they or girls they know were kept out of school or married young, or about their own or their family's schooling, journeys, country, religion or ethnicity.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners keep Kartini's 1901 hope, the 1903 government decision and what actually happened apart, and name a limit of an edited, translated letter. Evidence move (brief 3B): keep the sisters' 1901 school hope separate from the government's plan for girls' schools (in the same letter) and from the 1903 decision. A sound answer keeps the letter's aim, the official decision and the outcome distinct. Misconceptions to catch: merging the sisters' school plan with the government plan; thinking the decision proves she studied; treating one noble woman's letters as the voice of all girls in Java. Never invent a Kartini quotation; paraphrase only. Outcome details for teachers: in July 1903 Kartini and her sisters began teaching a few girls at home; in a letter of 24 July 1903 she asked whether the unused money could go instead to a gifted young student named Salim; she married the regent of Rembang later that year and died in 1904.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the 1921 English edition is a selection of about two-thirds of the 1911 Dutch book, which J.H. Abendanon edited; it carries colonial-era framing from the translator and a foreword, and the Dutch editor notes that some letters from mid-1903 were “not suitable for publication”. Separate Kartini's words from the editors'. Joost Coté's Kartini: The Complete Writings 1898–1904 (2014) is a fuller modern translation. The decision's details (7 July 1903, 4,800 guilders, study in Batavia for Kartini and Roekmini, not used) come from that Dutch edition; the National Archives of Indonesia's catalogue record of it could not be opened from here.
